abstract: Driven by national security concerns, a growing number of countries screen foreign investment in an expanding range of sectors, yet evidence on the economic effects of such screening is scarce. This column uses new sector-level data for 43 OECD and EU countries to show that screening reduces the number of cross-border acquisitions by 11–18% but leaves the total value of inward investment unchanged. There is evidence for re-structuring of deals: minority stakes fall while controlling acquisitions rise. The effects are not concentrated on investors from China or other politically non-aligned countries.

title: Investment screening reshapes rather than shrinks foreign investment

abstract: The European banking sector is known for high regulatory complexity, market fragmentation, and uneven implementation of international standards. However, this column argues that across-the-board reductions in capital requirements are not the solution. European requirements are not uniformly higher than US requirements, and capital rules do not mainly explain the past gap in return on equity, which is now largely closed. Lower capital requirements are also unlikely to unlock additional lending for early-stage technologies and innovative firms. Instead, reforms should focus on simplifying the interaction between different requirements, streamlining reporting, and completing the Banking Union.
title: Lower capital requirements are no shortcut to European competitiveness
